real_qa.q: Why did Pat McCrory implement a light rail system in Charlotte's South End instead of connecting to the airport?
real_qa.r: McCrory chose the South End because the numbers showed it could work best there. He had done extensive homework and determined that most people going to the airport do not come to downtown Charlotte, and the density was insufficient at the airport. He spent considerable time in Washington D.C. researching transportation solutions before making this decision.
real_qa.requete: Charlotte light rail South End airport why

real_qa.q: How did Pat McCrory reduce Charlotte's murder rate during his tenure as mayor?
real_qa.r: McCrory instituted a tolerate no truancy program, a teen curfew, and targeted the top 100 criminals in the city. He hired many police officers, put pressure on the governor and local district attorney to prosecute repeat offenders, and was very tough on crime overall. He brought the murder rate down from approximately 125-130 murders per year to 35 people per year.

real_qa.q: What was the Committee of 100 transportation report that influenced Pat McCrory's vision for Charlotte?
real_qa.r: McCrory found a notebook behind the credence in the mayor's office containing a general outline of a Committee of 100 report on transportation, including mass transit for the future. This report sparked his thinking about Charlotte's transportation needs and ultimately led to his decision to pursue a light rail project as an alternative to highway expansion.
real_qa.requete: Committee of 100 Charlotte transportation report McCrory

real_qa.q: How did Bill Lee of Duke Power influence Pat McCrory's entry into politics?
real_qa.r: Bill Lee, chairman and CEO of Duke Power, immediately supported McCrory when he expressed interest in running for city council. Lee introduced him to business leaders including Alan Dixon of Ruddock Corporation and helped him build visibility and connections. McCrory won his 1989 city council election at-large by 300 votes over Dick Prim.
real_qa.requete: Bill Lee Duke Power Pat McCrory city council 1989

real_qa.q: What advice did Bill Lee give Pat McCrory regarding timing for implementing major infrastructure projects?
real_qa.r: Lee told McCrory: You can do it now before the pain arrives, but it's going to be one hell of a sale, or you can wait for the pain to arrive and do it then, and it will be an easy sell but you've probably waited too long. Lee applied this metaphor to both transportation planning and his own health—he died a month later of a heart attack.
real_qa.requete: Bill Lee pain infrastructure timing quote McCrory

real_qa.q: Why did Andrew Dunn write an independent biography of Pat McCrory instead of an authorized memoir?
real_qa.r: Andrew Dunn approached McCrory unsolicited after mentioning in his newsletter that while other governors had books written about them, Pat McCrory did not. Dunn wanted to write an independent examination of McCrory's political career, not a puff piece. McCrory agreed because he wanted his record to be examined fairly with someone doing their homework, and the book covers the good, the bad, and the ugly of his political career.
real_qa.requete: Andrew Dunn Change Agent Pat McCrory independent biography

guest.bio_context: Pat McCrory was elected to the Charlotte City Council in 1989 and served a record 14 years as the city's mayor. He chaired the U.S. Conference of Mayors Environmental Committee for six terms, founded the North Carolina Metropolitan Coalition, and served on the U.S. Homeland Security Advisory Council. In 2012, he was elected the 74th governor of North Carolina, serving from 2013 to 2017, with a term defined by tax and regulatory overhaul and transportation investment. Since leaving office, he has been a radio personality on WBT radio in Charlotte.
